lines: BUTTERFLY FOREST. A public garden of the county council. Open from sunrise to sunset. Admission free.
Visitors are asked not to pick the flowers. Visitors are counted in at the gate and counted out again, and the two counts are to agree.

Under it, the plan of the gardens as they were. THE LAWN is inside THE GATE, and THE KEEPER'S HUT past it. THE RIDES go round the hut, and off them THE HEARTH, THE ROCKERY, THE MAZE, THE WATER GARDEN and THE STANDING STONE.
THE ROSE WALK is across THE WATER GARDEN, and THE GROTTO through THE MAZE. Butterflies are released at THE STANDING STONE, five at a time. Nets from THE KEEPER'S HUT.
Below, on a newer board, in a different hand, the paint run where it was done in a hurry: the paths have grown over. keep to the light.
Eleven glass cases on the wall, each labelled in the same careful hand. The labels are trades: CARTER. NURSE. SIGNALMAN.
Ten of them have something pinned inside, wings open. I don't look at the one marked NURSE for long.
The eleventh label is blank. The case is open, and there's a pin in it with nothing on the pin.
The case marked NIGHT WATCHMAN has no wings in it. On its pin, through the hole of a brass tally stamped G.M.Co., there's a key. I work it off the pin.
The eleventh label is blank, the case open, the pin bare. NIGHT WATCHMAN is empty now, and there's my thumbprint on the glass.
Eight, in the order the labels were written along the wall. I lay them out under the row to see. The blank label's the one they fit.
A charcoal burner's hearth, swept out, with the kettle still hung over it and next week's wood stacked ready.
The hedge is thick on three sides, with one way in. I can sleep here.
It settles on my sleeve and opens its wings out flat. I've nothing to keep it in.
It lets the net come right down over it. The wings are the colour of the inside of an old book, where the light's never got.
It comes onto the back of my hand and stays there. I'd need a net.
It's been on the same flower since I came in, and the flower's dead. It doesn't move when the net comes down.
It goes twice round my head and off again. I've nothing to catch it with.
It won't keep still. I put the net where it's going next and hold it there, and it flies in.
It sits on my cuff, wet through, and the cuff gets wet. I've nothing to put it in.
Wet to the wing tips, and the grass under it is dry.
It rides on my shoulder a few steps and gets off where the flowers lean. I'd want a net for this one.
The flowers in this glade lean when it goes over them, all one way, the way it went.
It sits on my sleeve and the cloth lights up under it. I've nothing to keep it in.
In the hollow it's the only light. It goes out while the net's closing, and comes back on inside it.
It comes out of the burnt tree and lands on my sleeve. I've nothing to keep it in.
It came out of the burnt tree. There's no soot on it anywhere, and the wings smell of nothing at all.
A moth bigger than my hand lands on my sleeve and holds on. I'd need a net, and I'd rather it was a big one.
Bigger than my hand, and it doesn't mind the lamp. It walks into the net on its legs.
A butterfly over the road by the forest gate. Its colours are the ones I saw floating past the window in the tunnel.
It keeps a little way ahead of me, then turns back toward the gate at the same spot each time. I listen for it, which is a silly thing to do with a butterfly.
THE GATE. Visitors are counted in and counted out here.
THE LAWN. The beds are planted where the sun comes down.
THE KEEPER'S HUT. Nets are issued here.
THE RIDES. Every garden opens off the rides.
THE HEARTH. A charcoal burner's. Visitors may rest by it.
THE ROCKERY. Mind the loose stone.
THE MAZE. Visitors are asked not to cut through the hedges.
THE WATER GARDEN. The footbridge is closed for repair.
THE STANDING STONE. Butterflies are released here, five at a time.
The path up to it has gone to bare earth.
